Name: Silver Beaker of Puzur-Sušinak (partially deciphered)
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Dialectics (Conflict)
Short Description: A hammered silver vessel bearing a Linear Elamite inscription associated with the ruler Puzur-Sušinak and the cult of Inšušinak at Susa. It belongs to the late third-millennium royal and votive culture in which kingship, temple dedication, and local identity were expressed together. A substantial decipherment of Linear Elamite has been proposed, but some readings and the extent of the decipherment remain debated.

Name: Kutik-Inshushinak Inscriptions
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Dialectics (Conflict), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Becoming (Process Ontology), Subversion (Negation)
Arts and Sciences Tags: Political Science / Law, History, Warfare, Education
Short Description: A corpus of royal building, dedicatory, and victory inscriptions associated with Kutik-Inšušinak, also known as Puzur-Sušinak, ruler of Susa and Anshan. The corpus uses Akkadian and Linear Elamite and combines Mesopotamian royal formulas with a distinct Elamite political and religious vocabulary. The texts document temple construction, military achievement, royal titles, and devotion to Inšušinak without requiring a simple narrative of cultural rejection or emancipation.

Name: Royal Inscriptions of Humban-Numena
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: Royal building and dedicatory inscriptions of the Middle Elamite king Humban-Numena, known from Susa and especially Liyan on the Persian Gulf. In the best-attested brick inscription, the king identifies himself as ruler of Anshan and Susa, credits divine favor for his kingship, and records rebuilding a sanctuary for Kiririša and the gods of Liyan. The corpus reflects temple patronage and dynastic legitimacy, not a verified royal land-grant charter.

Name: Shutruk-Nahhunte Inscription on the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin
Metaphysical Tags: Dialectics (Conflict), Subversion (Negation), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: The much older Akkadian victory monument of Naram-Sin was carried from Babylonia to Susa after an Elamite campaign under Shutruk-Nahhunte. The Elamite king added his own cuneiform inscription recording the seizure and dedicating the captured monument to Inšušinak. The object therefore preserves two distinct historical layers: an Akkadian royal image and text, followed centuries later by an Elamite statement of conquest and sacred appropriation.

Name: Yasna Haptanghaiti and Old Avestan Liturgy
Metaphysical Tags: Apophatic–Aporetic (Unknowable), Phenomenology (Experiential), Becoming (Process Ontology), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Monism (Single Principle), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: The Yasna Haptanghaiti, chiefly Yasna 35–41, is an Old Avestan prose liturgy preserved beside the Gathas within the later Yasna ritual. Its communal first-person prayers praise Ahura Mazda, Asha, the good creation, fire, waters, and earth. Together with associated Old Avestan prayers, it represents an early ritual layer transmitted orally by religious specialists. It is closely related to, but distinct from, the Gathas.

Short Description: Seventeen Old Avestan hymns arranged in five groups and embedded in the Yasna, traditionally attributed to Zarathustra. Their dense ritual-poetic speech addresses Ahura Mazda and explores Asha and Druj, moral choice, good thought, right action, judgment, and the fate of the worshipping community. They reflect an early Iranian religious environment and long oral transmission; they should not be reduced to a simple rejection of every older deity or ritual.

Short Description: Neo-Elamite inscriptions associated with the rock-relief sanctuaries around Malamir, modern Izeh, especially the long inscription of Hanni of Ayapir at Kul-e Farah I. Short Description: A selection from the Younger Avestan hymns addressed to individual sacred beings such as Mithra, Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā, Tištrya, and Verethragna. The surviving Yashts contain layers of different ages, combining praise, petition, ritual formula, cosmology, and heroic myth. They developed within an oral priestly tradition across much of the Old Iranian period and cannot be assigned as a single composition exclusively to the Achaemenid age.

Short Description: A monumental relief and trilingual inscription commissioned by Darius I at Behistun. It narrates his accession, the overthrow of Gaumata, and the suppression of rebellions across the empire, repeatedly crediting Ahuramazda and condemning rebellion through the language of the Lie. The text is both a historical narrative and a carefully constructed argument for dynastic legitimacy, obedience, and imperial order.

Name: Susa Foundation Inscriptions (Darius I)
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Short Description: The Susa palace inscriptions of Darius I, especially DSf and related foundation texts, describe royal construction under the protection of Ahuramazda. They enumerate materials and skilled workers drawn from many parts of the empire, presenting the palace as the product of coordinated imperial resources and expertise. The texts document building, geography, and royal ideology but do not by themselves establish a simple division between free and enslaved labor.

Short Description: A trilingual building inscription placed at the Gate of All Nations at Persepolis. Short Description: A trilingual royal inscription of Xerxes I from Persepolis, conventionally labeled XPh. After listing subject lands, Xerxes states that in one place daiva had been worshipped, that he destroyed that cult place, and that he established proper worship of Ahuramazda. The identity and location of the suppressed cult, its relationship to particular revolts, and the inscription’s implications for Achaemenid religion remain debated.

Name: Royal Inscriptions of Artaxerxes I and II
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism)
Short Description: A corpus of royal inscriptions issued under Artaxerxes I and Artaxerxes II at sites including Persepolis, Susa, and Ecbatana. They continue established Achaemenid formulas of genealogy, divine favor, royal authority, construction, and restoration. Some inscriptions of Artaxerxes II invoke Ahuramazda together with Anahita and Mithra. The corpus is evidence for continuity and adaptation in later Achaemenid kingship, not a neutral basis for claims of theatrical decline or routine bribery.

Name: Vendidad (Vidēvdād)
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Monism (Single Principle), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Subversion (Negation)
Short Description: A composite Younger Avestan work of twenty-two chapters whose name means the law or code repudiating the demons. Its opening chapters present a sacred geography and the story of Yima’s enclosure; later sections regulate purity, corpse handling, funerary practice, animals, medicine, offenses, penalties, and priestly procedure. Framed as dialogue between Ahura Mazda and Zarathustra, it preserves myth, ritual instruction, and legal reasoning transmitted orally before its later written and liturgical arrangement.
